# Cloning
Modern cloning rebuilds a body and imprints a stored neural pattern. It cannot prove that consciousness continued through death, and a clone remembers only what the template contained when it was recorded. Crescent law usually treats a certified restoration as the same legal person because titles, debts, contracts, oaths, and military responsibilities must remain administratively continuous.
Template freshness is unequal. Wealthy nobles, senior managers, and valuable specialists can update protected records frequently; an ordinary worker may wake with weeks or months missing. Repeated restoration can also cause memory overlap, compulsions, identity rejection, and [bold]sleeve drift[/bold], whose severe form is called [bold]Sleever Psychosis[/bold].
Anchor Vaults can preserve templates through severe Turning conditions, but a local cloning network still needs power, biomass, viable records, and current-cycle calibration.
## Practical use
If all else fails, patients will need to be cloned. This should only be used as a last resort, if recovery is impossible. This is most often the case when the body has started to rot, or if they have excessive amounts of damage.
Cloning itself is relatively simple. (Assuming the network is set.) Just drag a body into the scanner, check the cloning console, and clone! If they've taken cellular damage, or have rotted for too long, the results can be... less than pleasant.
As a note: Cloning isn't always available, and it would be best not to rely on it. Epistemics might be able to set up cloning, if it's unavailable.
## Biomass Creating a clone requires biomass, which, gruesomely, involves recycling organic material. Be it crew members without a soul, station pets, or hostile creatures that have been 'taken care of', things can often be recycled.
Dragging a body onto the biomass reclaimer (with your cursor) will mulch it for re-use. If it's a crew member, it's common practice to strip the body and return departmental gear before doing such.
